# Cascade: animation library for Unity UI Toolkit

> Cascade animates Unity UI Toolkit VisualElements (UXML/USS, UIElements) at runtime: tweens, easing, springs, stagger, enter/exit and screen transitions, hover/press/focus, named states, a no-code UI Animator and validated JSON animation sequences. Unity 6000.0+, pure C#, no dependencies. Cascade Lite is free and MIT licensed (https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/slug/394764); Cascade Pro adds springs, stagger, transitions, interactions, variants, the UI Animator, JSON sequences and effects (https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/slug/394760). Agent skill: npx skills add twitchedd/cascade-skill

This file is every page of the Cascade docs as plain Markdown, in reading order, so an assistant can
load the whole reference in one request. Each page starts with its URL.


---

# Cascade docs: the animation library for Unity UI Toolkit
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/

Cascade is an animation library for Unity UI Toolkit. It animates any `VisualElement` at runtime with one line of C#: fades, moves, scales, colors, sizes, springs, staggered lists and screen transitions.

It works with UXML/USS and UI Toolkit (UIElements) in Unity 6000.0 and later. It has no third-party dependencies and allocates nothing per frame. It doesn't support uGUI (Canvas).

```csharp
using Cascade;

panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
     .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);   // both run together
```

## Lite and Pro

Cascade comes in two tiers. Lite is free and MIT licensed, and covers the tween engine. Pro is a superset: it includes everything in Lite and adds the parts that are hard to write yourself.

| Feature | Lite (free) | Pro |
|---|---|---|
| Fade, move, scale, rotate, colors, width/height, top/left | yes | yes |
| Full easing set and `AnimationCurve` easing | yes | yes |
| Sequencing (`Then`), delays, loops, pause/resume/cancel | yes | yes |
| `await` any animation | yes | yes |
| Reduced-motion setting | yes | yes |
| Physics springs that keep momentum when interrupted | no | yes |
| Stagger across a list of elements | no | yes |
| Enter/exit and screen transitions (`Show`, `Hide`, `SwapTo`) | no | yes |
| Hover, press and focus animations | no | yes |
| Named states (variants) | no | yes |
| No-code UI Animator component with live preview in edit mode | no | yes |
| Drop shadow and glow elements | no | yes |

Each page marks Pro-only code with Pro. Everything else works in both.

Get Cascade Lite (free) Get Cascade Pro

# Getting started with Cascade: animate Unity UI Toolkit in one line
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/getting-started.html

Install the package, open the demo to see every feature running, then animate your first element.

## 1. Install

1. Add Cascade Lite (free) or Cascade Pro to your assets on the Unity Asset Store.
2. In Unity, open **Window ▸ Package Manager** and select **My Assets**.
3. Find Cascade and install it into your project.

Cascade needs Unity 6000.0 or later and runs on UI Toolkit only.

```sh
npx skills add twitchedd/cascade-skill
```

## 2. Open the demo

The demo is the fastest way to see what Cascade does. Every section shows an animation next to the code that makes it.

1. In the Package Manager, select Cascade and open the **Samples** tab.
2. Click **Import** next to the demo (Demo - Lite Gallery in Lite, Demo - Motion Gallery in Pro).
3. Open the scene in `Assets/Samples/` and press Play.

## 3. Animate an element

Add `using Cascade;` and call `Animate()` on any `VisualElement`. Durations are in seconds.

```csharp
using Cascade;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UIElements;

public class Intro : MonoBehaviour
{
    void OnEnable()
    {
        var root = GetComponent<UIDocument>().rootVisualElement;
        var card = root.Q("card");

        card.Animate()
            .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
            .Then()
            .MoveY(0f, 0.4f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutBack);
    }
}
```

Verbs in the same step run **together**. `Then()` starts the next step after the current one finishes.

`From(v)` sets where a verb starts. Without it, Cascade starts from the element's current value, so a card that is already visible has nothing to fade.

## 4. Control it

`Animate()` returns a handle you can keep:

```csharp
var pulse = badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.15f, 0.5f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong, 0); // 0 = forever

pulse.Pause();
pulse.Resume();
pulse.Cancel();          // stops where it is
badge.StopAnimations();  // stops everything on this element
```

Cancelling leaves the element where it is and does not call `OnComplete`. An animation that finishes on its own snaps to its target and calls `OnComplete`. Animations also cancel themselves when the element leaves the panel, so nothing writes to a closed screen.

## 5. Run code when it ends

```csharp
row.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.3f).OnSettled(completed => PaintSelection());
```

Use `OnSettled` for anything the player must see. It runs whether the animation finished or was cancelled. `OnComplete` doesn't run when a new animation replaces this one halfway, which happens whenever the player clicks quickly.

Or `await` it. The result is `true` when it finished and `false` when it was cancelled:

```csharp
async void PlayIntro()
{
    if (!await title.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.4f).From(0f)) return;   // the screen closed: stop
    await subtitle.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0.35f).From(20f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}
```

## What each verb animates

| Verb | Animates | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Fade` | opacity | 0 to 1 |
| `MoveX`, `MoveY`, `MoveTo` | translate | pixels; no layout cost |
| `NudgeX`, `NudgeY` | translate, additive | adds to a move that is already running |
| `ScaleTo` | scale | a multiplier; scales around `transform-origin` |
| `Rotate` | rotate | degrees |
| `SlideIn` | translate from an edge | `Edge.Top`, `Bottom`, `Left`, `Right` |
| `BackgroundColor`, `TextColor` | colors |  |
| `Width`, `Height`, `Size`, `Top`, `Left` | layout | re-runs layout each frame; use for accordions, not for many elements |
| `Value` | any float you choose | for counters, progress bars, custom properties |

## Next

- [How to animate a UI Toolkit VisualElement](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/animate-visualelement.html): how this compares with USS transitions and the scheduler.
- [Recipes](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/recipes.html): copy-and-paste patterns for common UI.

# How to animate a UI Toolkit VisualElement in Unity (USS transitions, scheduler, tweens)
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/animate-visualelement.html

Unity UI Toolkit has three built-in ways to animate a `VisualElement` at runtime: USS transitions, the panel scheduler, and the experimental animation API. They cover simple cases. For sequences, lists and interruptible motion, most projects end up writing their own tween layer or using a library.

This page shows each option with working code and when to use it.

| Approach | Good for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| USS transitions | hover and state changes styled in USS | no sequencing, no completion callback beyond an event, needs a frame before it runs on a new element |
| Panel scheduler | one custom effect | you write easing, timing, cancelling and cleanup yourself |
| `experimental.animation` | quick one-off tweens | experimental API that can change between Unity versions; durations in milliseconds |
| A tween library (Cascade) | sequences, lists, springs, transitions | a package to add |

## 1. USS transitions

Declare which properties animate in USS, then change the element's class from C#. UI Toolkit animates between the two styles.

```css
.panel {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 24px;
    transition-property: opacity, translate;
    transition-duration: 0.3s;
    transition-timing-function: ease-out-cubic;
}
.panel--open {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
}
```

```csharp
panel.EnableInClassList("panel--open", true);
```

This is the right tool for hover states and simple toggles, because the styling lives in USS with the rest of your look.

**Things to know:**

- A class added in the same frame the element is created doesn't animate: the element has no previous style to animate from yet. Wait a frame, for example with `panel.schedule.Execute(() => panel.AddToClassList("panel--open"))`.
- There's no built-in way to run step B after step A, or to start ten list items one after another.
- To react when it ends, register for `TransitionEndEvent`. It fires once per property; an interrupted transition sends `TransitionCancelEvent` instead.

## 2. The panel scheduler

Every element has a scheduler that runs code on the panel's update. You can drive any style value from it:

```csharp
void FadeIn(VisualElement el, float duration)
{
    float start = Time.unscaledTime;
    IVisualElementScheduledItem item = null;
    item = el.schedule.Execute(() =>
    {
        if (el.panel == null) { item.Pause(); return; }   // the element left the screen
        float t = Mathf.Clamp01((Time.unscaledTime - start) / duration);
        float eased = 1f - Mathf.Pow(1f - t, 3f);          // ease-out cubic
        el.style.opacity = eased;
        if (t >= 1f) item.Pause();
    }).Every(0);
}
```

This gives you full control, and it's what most hand-written UI Toolkit tweening looks like. The cost is that every effect repeats the same work: easing, the start value, stopping a previous animation on the same element, and stopping when the element is removed. Most projects end up wrapping it in a small tween helper, which grows into a library over time.

## 3. The experimental animation API

UI Toolkit includes a small tween API under `element.experimental.animation`:

```csharp
using UnityEngine.UIElements.Experimental;

el.experimental.animation
  .Start(new StyleValues { opacity = 0f }, new StyleValues { opacity = 1f }, 300)   // milliseconds
  .Ease(Easing.OutCubic);
```

It works for one-off tweens. It sits in the `Experimental` namespace, so it can change between Unity versions, and it has no sequencing, staggering or springs.

## 4. A tween library: Cascade

Cascade is a runtime animation library built for UI Toolkit. The same fade-and-rise as above is one call, and it handles the parts the scheduler version leaves to you: easing, start values, replacing an animation that's already running, and cancelling when the element leaves the panel.

```csharp
using Cascade;

panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
     .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
```

Sequences chain with `Then()`, and every animation can be awaited:

```csharp
await title.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.4f).From(0f);
await button.Animate().ScaleTo(1f, 0.3f).From(0.8f).Ease(Ease.OutBack);
```

Cascade Lite is free and MIT licensed, and covers everything on this page. [Springs](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/spring-animation.html), [staggered lists](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/stagger-list.html) and [screen transitions](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/transitions.html) are in Pro.

Get Cascade Lite (free) Getting started

## Which one should you use?

- **A hover color or a toggle styled in USS:** USS transitions.
- **One unusual effect, such as a custom shader value:** the scheduler, or Cascade's `Value` verb.
- **Panels that slide in, then something else happens:** a tween library, so the steps run in order and stop cleanly.
- **Lists, interruptible buttons, screen changes:** a library with stagger, springs and transitions.

Animate `translate`, `scale`, `rotate` and `opacity` where you can. They don't trigger layout. Animating `width`, `height`, `top` or `left` re-runs layout every frame, which is fine for one accordion but slow for many elements.

---

# Spring animation in Unity UI Toolkit (physics springs for VisualElements)
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/spring-animation.html

Unity UI Toolkit has no spring animation built in. USS transitions and the experimental animation API only offer fixed-duration easing curves. You can write a small spring yourself on the panel scheduler, or use a library: Cascade Pro adds a spring to any animation in one call.

A spring moves an element toward its target like a physical object: it speeds up, can overshoot, and settles. Its length comes from its stiffness rather than a fixed duration. The real reason to use one is interruption. When a new target arrives halfway, a spring keeps its current speed and turns toward the new target. An eased tween has to start again from zero speed, which shows as a hitch. Anything the player can click rapidly, drag or toggle looks better on a spring.

## Without a library: a spring on the scheduler

Every `VisualElement` has a scheduler that can run code each frame. A damped spring is a few lines of math on top of it:

```csharp
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UIElements;

public static class SimpleSpring
{
    // Springs el's horizontal position to targetX. Each call starts again from zero speed.
    public static IVisualElementScheduledItem SpringToX(VisualElement el, float targetX,
                                                        float stiffness = 300f, float damping = 22f)
    {
        float x = el.resolvedStyle.translate.x, velocity = 0f;
        IVisualElementScheduledItem tick = null;
        tick = el.schedule.Execute(() =>
        {
            float dt = Mathf.Min(Time.unscaledDeltaTime, 1f / 30f);   // keep a frame hitch from exploding it
            velocity += (stiffness * (targetX - x) - damping * velocity) * dt;
            x += velocity * dt;
            el.style.translate = new Translate(x, 0);
            if (Mathf.Abs(targetX - x) < 0.01f && Mathf.Abs(velocity) < 0.01f)
            {
                el.style.translate = new Translate(targetX, 0);
                tick.Pause();                                          // settled
            }
        }).Every(0);
        return tick;
    }
}
```

This is fine for one property and one target. It gets harder from there:

- It starts from zero speed on every call, so a quick second click shows the hitch a spring is meant to remove. Keeping the speed means storing it per element and pausing the previous run.
- Scale, rotation, colour and size each need their own version.
- Nothing stops it when the element leaves the panel, and two runs on the same element fight each other.
- Stiffness and damping are hard to tune by eye.

## With Cascade: a spring on any verb Pro

```csharp
using Cascade;

card.Animate().ScaleTo(1.2f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Bouncy);
panel.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0f).From(40f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy);
```

`Spring()` replaces the verb's duration: the spring decides how long it takes, so pass `0f` as the duration.

| Preset | Feel | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `SpringPreset.Gentle` | slow, smooth, no visible bounce | large panels, backgrounds |
| `SpringPreset.Snappy` | quick, settles fast | buttons, menus, most UI |
| `SpringPreset.Bouncy` | overshoots and wobbles | rewards, playful buttons, game UI |

## A custom spring, described by feel

Tuning stiffness and damping by hand is slow. `SpringConfig.FromResponse` takes two numbers that match what you see:

```csharp
// response: roughly how long one swing takes, in seconds (0.15 = a quick control, 0.5 = a large panel)
// bounce:   0 = no overshoot, toward 1 = very bouncy
var drawer = SpringConfig.FromResponse(0.4f, 0.15f);
sidePanel.Animate().MoveX(0f, 0f).Spring(drawer);
```

If you already know the physics values, use `new SpringConfig(stiffness, damping, mass)`.

## Interruptions that keep momentum

```csharp
// Call this on every click. No StopAnimations() first, on purpose.
void Flip()
{
    _flip = !_flip;
    card.Animate().MoveX(_flip ? 90f : -90f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Bouncy);
}
```

Click quickly and the card turns around smoothly instead of stopping dead each time. The animation that is replaced hands its current velocity to the new one. Call `StopAnimations()` first only when you want a hard reset, because it drops the velocity too.

## Springs on hover and press

```csharp
playButton.OnHover().ScaleTo(1.12f, 0f).WithSpring(SpringPreset.Bouncy);
playButton.OnPress().ScaleTo(0.94f, 0.08f);
```

Moving the pointer on and off quickly keeps the motion continuous, for the same reason as above.

## Springs in a sequence

```csharp
card.Animate()
    .MoveY(-40f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
    .Then().ScaleTo(1.1f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Bouncy)
    .Then().MoveY(0f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy);
```

A spring step ends when the spring has settled, then the next step starts.

## When not to use a spring

- **Exact timing:** a progress bar or something synced to audio needs a fixed duration. Use an ease.
- **Fades:** opacity has nothing to overshoot. An ease reads cleaner.
- **Exits:** things leaving the screen usually look better accelerating away with `Ease.InCubic`.

---

# Stagger animation in Unity UI Toolkit: animate list items one after another
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/stagger-list.html

A stagger plays the same animation on each item of a list, each one starting a little later than the one before, so a menu or a list of results reads as one movement instead of a block appearing at once. In UI Toolkit you can build one from USS transitions with a delay per item, or use Cascade Pro, which does it in one chained call.

## Without a library: USS transitions with a delay per item

Put the hidden and shown states in USS, give each item a longer `transition-delay` from C#, then add the "shown" class:

```css
.row {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 40px 0;
    transition-property: opacity, translate;
    transition-duration: 0.35s;
    transition-timing-function: ease-out-cubic;
}
.row.shown {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
}
```

```csharp
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using UnityEngine.UIElements;

var items = listRoot.Query<VisualElement>(className: "row").ToList();
for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++)
    items[i].style.transitionDelay = new List<TimeValue> { new TimeValue(i * 0.06f, TimeUnit.Second) };

// Add the class on the next frame. Added in the same frame the element appears, UI Toolkit skips the transition.
listRoot.schedule.Execute(() => items.ForEach(e => e.AddToClassList("shown")));
```

This works with no extra code in your project. Its limits:

- The timing lives in two files, and the delays stay on the items, so hiding the list again staggers too unless you reset them.
- Items must start hidden in USS. Items that are already visible don't animate.
- There is no single "the whole list has finished" moment: each item sends its own `TransitionEndEvent`.
- A transition can't spring, and changing the list halfway leaves items mid-transition.

## With Cascade: one call Pro

```csharp
using Cascade;
using System.Linq;

var items = listRoot.Query<VisualElement>(className: "row").ToList();

items.AnimateEach()
     .SlideIn(Edge.Right, 0.35f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
     .Fade(1f, 0.35f).From(0f)
     .Stagger(0.06f);              // item i starts i × 0.06 s after the first
```

`AnimateEach()` works on any list of `VisualElement`s, so the result of a UQuery works directly.

Write `From(0f)` on the fade. Each item starts from its own value when its turn comes, and an item that is already visible has nothing to fade. `From` also hides the later items right away, so they don't flash before their turn.

## Choosing the step

- **0.04–0.08 s** per item works for most menus and lists.
- Above about **0.1 s** a long list starts to feel slow.
- The whole group takes `duration + (count − 1) × step`, so it grows with the list.

For lists whose length changes, fix the total time instead of the step:

```csharp
// spread the whole list over 0.4 s, but never more than 0.06 s between items
float step = Stagger.StepForSpan(items.Count, 0.4f, 0.06f);
items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Stagger(step);
```

## Start something after the list

```csharp
float total = Stagger.TotalDuration(items.Count, 0.35f, 0.06f);
footer.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.25f).From(0f).Delay(total);
```

## Replaying the list

When the list is shown again, stop what is still running on the items first, so a quick re-open starts cleanly:

```csharp
foreach (var item in items) item.StopAnimations();
items.AnimateEach().SlideIn(Edge.Right, 0.35f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic).Fade(1f, 0.35f).From(0f).Stagger(0.06f);
```

## Staggering with Cascade Lite

Lite has no `AnimateEach`, but it has `Delay`. A loop gives the same result for a short list:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++)
{
    items[i].Animate()
        .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Delay(i * 0.06f)
        .SlideIn(Edge.Right, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic).Delay(i * 0.06f);
}
```

Pro's `AnimateEach` adds the timing helpers above, works with springs, and handles replays and cancelling for the whole group.

Get Cascade Pro Get Cascade Lite (free)

---

# Enter, exit and screen transitions in Unity UI Toolkit
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/transitions.html

An enter/exit transition animates an element as it appears and disappears. The tricky part in UI Toolkit is `display`: an element must be `display: flex` before it can animate in, and should become `display: none` only after it has animated out, or it keeps taking space and catching clicks.

Cascade Pro's `Show` and `Hide` handle that order for you.

```csharp
using Cascade;

panel.Show(Transition.SlideFade(Edge.Bottom, 0.35f));   // display: flex, then animate in
panel.Hide(Transition.ScaleFade(0.25f));                // animate out, then display: none
```

## Built-in transitions

| Transition | Looks like |
|---|---|
| `Transition.Fade(d)` | opacity only |
| `Transition.Slide(edge, d)` | moves in from an edge |
| `Transition.SlideFade(edge, d)` | moves and fades; the usual choice for panels and toasts |
| `Transition.Scale(d)` | grows from 85% |
| `Transition.ScaleFade(d)` | grows and fades; the usual choice for dialogs |
| `Transition.Crossfade(d)` | a fade, used for swapping screens |

Add `.WithEase(...)` to any of them, for example `Transition.ScaleFade(0.28f).WithEase(Ease.OutBack)`.

## Toast: slide in, dismiss itself

```csharp
void ShowToast()
{
    toast.StopAnimations();   // a second click restarts it cleanly
    toast.Show(Transition.SlideFade(Edge.Top, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic));
    toast.schedule.Execute(HideToast).ExecuteLater(1900);
}

void HideToast()
{
    if (toast.resolvedStyle.display == DisplayStyle.None) return;
    toast.Hide(Transition.SlideFade(Edge.Top, 0.25f).WithEase(Ease.InCubic));
}
```

Ease out on the way in and ease in on the way out. Accelerating away reads as "dismissed".

## Modal dialog with a dimmed backdrop

```csharp
void OpenModal()
{
    modalOpen = true;
    modalRoot.style.display = DisplayStyle.Flex;
    backdrop.Show(Transition.Fade(0.2f));
    dialog.Show(Transition.ScaleFade(0.28f).WithEase(Ease.OutBack));
}

void CloseModal()
{
    modalOpen = false;
    backdrop.Hide(Transition.Fade(0.18f));
    dialog.Hide(Transition.ScaleFade(0.2f));
    // hide the container after the children finish, unless the modal was re-opened meanwhile
    modalRoot.schedule.Execute(() => { if (!modalOpen) modalRoot.style.display = DisplayStyle.None; })
             .ExecuteLater(240);
}
```

Keep the backdrop on a plain fade and give the overshoot to the dialog, so only one thing draws the eye.

## Swap screens

```csharp
screens.SwapTo(settingsScreen, Transition.Crossfade(0.3f));
```

`SwapTo` animates the current child of `screens` out (ending at `display: none`) and the new one in. Both screens must already be children of `screens`.

## Tabs with a sliding underline

```csharp
void SwitchTab(int i)
{
    if (i == current) return;                        // clicking the open tab does nothing
    pages[current].Hide(Transition.Fade(0.16f));     // out a little faster than in
    pages[i].Show(Transition.Fade(0.22f));

    indicator.Animate().MoveX(tabs[i].layout.x, 0.28f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
    indicator.Animate().Width(tabs[i].layout.width, 0.28f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
    current = i;
}
```

Read `layout` only after the first layout pass, for example in a `GeometryChangedEvent` callback. Before that it returns zeros.

## Show/Hide or AnimateIn/AnimateOut?

`AnimateIn` and `AnimateOut` play the same transitions but don't touch `display`. Use them when you manage visibility yourself. Anything that opens and closes repeatedly should use `Show` and `Hide`: an element left at `display: none` by a previous `Hide` stays invisible under `AnimateIn`.

## With Cascade Lite

Lite has no `Show`/`Hide`, but the same effect takes a few lines:

```csharp
// in
panel.style.display = DisplayStyle.Flex;
panel.Animate().SlideIn(Edge.Bottom, 0.35f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic).Fade(1f, 0.35f).From(0f);

// out
panel.Animate().Fade(0f, 0.25f).Ease(Ease.InCubic)
     .OnSettled(done => { if (done) panel.style.display = DisplayStyle.None; });
// "done" is false when a new animation replaced this one, e.g. the panel was opened again
```

Get Cascade Pro Get Cascade Lite (free)

---

# Unity UI Toolkit animation recipes: hover, accordion, states, async, loops
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/recipes.html

Short patterns for common UI, each one taken from the demo that ships with the package. Toasts, modals, tabs and screen swaps are on the [transitions page](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/transitions.html), and lists on the [stagger page](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/stagger-list.html).

## Hover, press and focus Pro

```csharp
playButton.OnHover().ScaleTo(1.08f, 0.12f, Ease.OutBack);
playButton.OnPress().ScaleTo(0.94f, 0.08f);
playButton.OnFocus().ScaleTo(1.08f, 0.15f, Ease.OutBack);   // keyboard and gamepad get the same feedback
```

Declare these once when you set up the screen, not inside event handlers. Pair `OnHover` with `OnFocus`, or the feedback only works with a mouse.

## Accordion

```csharp
void ToggleAccordion()
{
    open = !open;
    body.Animate().Height(open ? 168f : 0f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}
```

Give the body `overflow: hidden` in USS so its contents are clipped while it closes. `Height` re-runs layout every frame, which is what an accordion needs; for many elements at once, prefer `MoveX`, `ScaleTo` and `Rotate`, which don't.

## Named states Pro

```csharp
card.Variants()
    .State("normal",   s => s.ScaleTo(1f).RotateTo(0f).FadeTo(1f).In(0.35f).WithSpring(SpringPreset.Snappy))
    .State("featured", s => s.ScaleTo(1.2f).RotateTo(-5f).FadeTo(1f).In(0.35f).WithSpring(SpringPreset.Bouncy))
    .State("dim",      s => s.ScaleTo(0.9f).RotateTo(0f).FadeTo(0.4f).In(0.3f).With(Ease.OutCubic));

card.To("featured");   // later, from anywhere
```

Declare each state once and move between them by name. Selection, difficulty pickers and inventory slots fit this well: three states cost three declarations, not a transition for every pair.

## A sequence with async/await

```csharp
async void PlayIntro()
{
    bool finished = await title.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.4f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
    if (!finished) return;   // cancelled: the screen closed, so stop here
    await subtitle.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0.35f).From(20f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
    await startButton.Animate().ScaleTo(1f, 0.3f).From(0.8f).Ease(Ease.OutBack);
}
```

Always check the result. An intro that continues after its screen has closed is a common source of errors. Await each animation once; keep the result if you need it again.

Without async, `Then()` does the same and allocates nothing:

```csharp
card.Animate()
    .MoveY(-40f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
    .Then().MoveY(0f, 0.5f).Delay(0.6f).Ease(Ease.OutBounce);   // rise, hold 0.6 s, fall
```

## Loops

```csharp
var pulse = badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.15f, 0.5f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong, 0);  // 0 = forever
spinner.Animate().Rotate(360f, 1f).Loop(LoopMode.Restart, 0);
```

Keep the handle of a loop that runs forever. Without it, the only way to stop it is `StopAnimations()` on the element.

## Bump something that is already moving

```csharp
ship.Animate().MoveX(400f, 2f);           // a long move
ship.Animate().NudgeY(-12f, 0.15f);       // a hit: adds a bump without stopping the move
```

`MoveX` on an element that is already moving replaces that movement. `Nudge`, `NudgeX` and `NudgeY` add on top of it instead, which is what screen shake and hit reactions need.

## Count a number up

```csharp
int from = shown, to = coins;
scoreLabel.Animate().Value(0f, 1f, 0.6f, t => scoreLabel.text = Mathf.RoundToInt(Mathf.Lerp(from, to, t)).ToString())
          .Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
```

## Respect reduced motion

```csharp
MotionSettings.Mode = MotionMode.Reduced;   // Full, Reduced, Crossfade or None
```

Set it once from your accessibility settings. Every animation started afterwards follows it: `Reduced` shortens and calms motion, `Crossfade` replaces movement with fades, and `None` jumps to the end values. Callbacks and `await` still complete, so game logic waiting on an animation keeps working.

For motion that carries meaning, such as a loading spinner, opt out:

```csharp
spinner.Animate().Rotate(360f, 1f).Loop(LoopMode.Restart, 0).IgnoreReducedMotion();
```

## Common mistakes

| What you see | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The fade does nothing | The element is already at the target value | Add `From(0f)` |
| It animates but stays invisible | A previous `Hide()` left it at `display: none` | Use `Show()`, not `AnimateIn()` |
| `layout.x` or `layout.width` is 0 | Read before the first layout pass | Read it in a `GeometryChangedEvent` callback |
| `OnComplete` never runs | The animation was cancelled or replaced, not finished | Use `OnSettled`, which runs either way |
| A bump stops the movement | `MoveX` replaces the running move | Use `NudgeX` |
| The animation stops when a screen closes | The element left the panel | Intended: Cascade cancels it so nothing writes to a closed screen |
| A staggered list feels slow | The step is too large | 0.04–0.08 s between items |

---

# Animate Unity UI Toolkit without code: the Cascade UI Animator
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/no-code.html

The UI Animator component lets designers add motion to a UI Toolkit screen from the Inspector: pick the elements, pick when, pick a preset, and preview it without entering Play mode.

## Before you start

The screen must be a UI Toolkit UI: a GameObject with a **UIDocument** component pointing at a UXML file. Give the elements you want to animate a name or a USS class in UI Builder, for example `hero-card` or `menu-item`.

## Add motion in six steps

1. **Add the component.** Select the GameObject with the UIDocument, then **Add Component ▸ Cascade ▸ UI Animator**.
2. **Add a rule.** Click **+** in the Rules list. A rule reads as one sentence: these elements, on this trigger, play this.
3. **Choose the elements.** Click the ▾ next to the selector. It lists every element name and USS class in your UXML, with how many elements each matches. Or type one: `#hero-card` targets one named element, `.menu-item` targets every element with that class.
4. **Choose when.** **OnEnable** plays once when the screen appears (entrances). **Hover**, **Press** and **Focus** react to the pointer and keyboard.
5. **Choose what.** Pick a preset with ▾, or choose **Create New…** to make one in place.
6. **Preview.** Click ▶ on the rule. It plays in the Game view and then restores the elements. Adjust the preset and press ▶ again.

## Presets

Presets are assets you reuse across screens and projects. Create them from **Assets ▸ Create ▸ Cascade**.

| Preset | Use it for | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| Transition Preset | entrances and exits | fade, slide from an edge, scale; one duration; an ease or a spring |
| Interaction Preset | hover, press and focus | scale, fade, rotate to an "active" look |
| Sequence Preset | multi-step choreography | steps that run in order, each with actions that run together; every verb, each with its own timing, ease or spring |

A rule's Sequence slot wins over its simple preset. Name presets by intent, such as `Entrance-SlideUp`, `Hover-Lift` or `Press-Squish`, and keep them in one folder so the motion style travels with you.

## Lists

When a selector matches several elements (such as `.menu-item`), set **stagger** on the rule: the seconds between each element's start. `0.06` gives the classic menu cascade. Stagger applies to OnEnable rules.

## Warnings

The Inspector warns about rules that would do nothing: an empty selector, a missing preset, a preset with no channels enabled, or a hover that only fades to full opacity (elements already rest there). No warnings means the rule will do something visible.

## Troubleshooting

- **Nothing happens on ▶:** the console says the selector matched nothing. Fix the name or class, or pick from the ▾ list.
- **Nothing happens in Play mode:** the preset changes nothing visible. Enable a channel.
- **Hover doesn't react:** live pointer input needs Play mode. ▶ previews the motion any time.
- **An element is stuck halfway in edit mode:** previews restore styles when they finish. If Unity was interrupted mid-preview, reopen the scene; edit-mode styles are never saved.

## What still needs code

- Connecting [reduced motion](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/recipes.html#respect-reduced-motion) to your settings menu: one line.
- [Named states](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/recipes.html) and [screen swaps](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/transitions.html).
- Motion triggered by gameplay events. A developer can play any preset from code: `myPreset.Play(element)`.

---

# Drop shadow and glow in Unity UI Toolkit, and animated blur and tint
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/effects.html

UI Toolkit has no box-shadow. Cascade Pro adds a drop shadow and glow element drawn with a mesh, and on Unity 6.3 and later it animates the USS `filter` blur and tint.

## Drop shadow

`DropShadowElement` draws a soft shadow behind its children. Put the element you want shadowed inside it.

```csharp
using Cascade;

var shadow = new DropShadowElement
{
    shadowColor = new Color(0f, 0f, 0f, 0.5f),
    blur = 22f,      // how far the edge fades, in pixels
    spread = 2f,     // grows the shadow before the fade
    offsetY = 12f,   // pushes it down, like light from above
};
shadow.style.width = 110;
shadow.style.height = 90;
shadow.Add(card);
```

It is also a UXML element, so you can add it to a layout in UI Builder and set its color, blur, spread and offsets there.

## Glow

A glow is the same element with no offset and a bright color:

```csharp
var glow = new DropShadowElement { shadowColor = new Color(1f, 0.6f, 0.2f, 0.8f), blur = 18f, spread = 4f, offsetY = 0f };
glow.Add(rewardIcon);
```

It's mesh-drawn: no shaders and any render pipeline. Each one costs an extra draw, which is fine for a few hero cards and buttons, not for every row of a long list.

## Animated blur and tint (Unity 6.3+)

Unity 6.3 added a `filter` property to UI Toolkit. Cascade animates two of its functions as verbs:

```csharp
background.Animate().BlurTo(8f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);              // blur radius in pixels
icon.Animate().TintTo(new Color(1f, 0.4f, 0.4f), 0.2f);                 // flash red
```

Other filter functions already on the element are kept. A filter re-renders the element every frame it animates, so measure it on your target devices. On Unity versions before 6.3 these verbs compile and do nothing, with a single console warning, so shared code stays portable.

---

# Framer Motion for Unity UI Toolkit: concepts mapped to Cascade
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/framer-motion.html

UI Toolkit borrowed CSS from the web, and Cascade borrows its animation model from Framer Motion. If you know one, here is the other.

| Framer Motion | Cascade | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| `animate={{ opacity: 1, x: 0 }}` | `el.Animate().Fade(1f, .3f).MoveX(0f, .3f)` | Lite |
| `initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 24 }}` | `.From(0f)` after each verb | Lite |
| `transition={{ duration: .3, ease: "easeOut" }}` | duration on each verb, `.Ease(Ease.OutCubic)` | Lite |
| `transition={{ type: "spring", stiffness, damping }}` | `.Spring(new SpringConfig(stiffness, damping))` or `SpringPreset.Snappy` | Pro |
| `transition={{ type: "spring", visualDuration, bounce }}` | `.WithResponse(response, bounce)` | Pro |
| Interruptions keep velocity | Built in: a replaced spring hands its velocity to the new one | Pro |
| `variants` + `animate="open"` | `el.Variants().State("open", s => …)`, then `el.To("open")` | Pro |
| `whileHover={{ scale: 1.05 }}` | `el.OnHover().ScaleTo(1.05f, .15f)` | Pro |
| `whileTap={{ scale: .96 }}` | `el.OnPress().ScaleTo(.96f, .08f)` | Pro |
| `whileFocus` | `el.OnFocus()` | Pro |
| `staggerChildren: .05` | `items.AnimateEach()….Stagger(.05f)` | Pro |
| `<AnimatePresence>` enter/exit | `el.Show(Transition…)` / `el.Hide(Transition…)` | Pro |
| Page transitions | `container.SwapTo(screen, Transition.Crossfade(.3f))` | Pro |
| `useReducedMotion()` | `MotionSettings.Mode = MotionMode.Reduced` | Lite |
| `onAnimationComplete` | `.OnComplete(…)`, or `.OnSettled(…)` to also hear about cancels | Lite |
| `useAnimate` controls | the chain is the handle: `h.Pause()`, `h.Resume()`, `h.Cancel()` | Lite |
| `await animate(…)` | `await el.Animate()…` (returns whether it finished) | Lite |

## A button, ported

```text
// Framer Motion
<motion.button
  initial={{ opacity: 0, y: 24 }}
  animate={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}
  whileHover={{ scale: 1.05 }}
  whileTap={{ scale: 0.96 }}
  transition={{ type: "spring", stiffness: 210, damping: 22 }} />
```

```csharp
// Cascade
button.OnHover().ScaleTo(1.05f, 0.15f, Ease.OutBack);
button.OnPress().ScaleTo(0.96f, 0.08f);
button.Animate()
      .Fade(1f, 0f).From(0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy)
      .MoveY(0f, 0f).From(24f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy);
```

## Differences worth knowing

- **Durations are seconds,** like Framer Motion, not milliseconds like Unity's own scheduler.
- **Verbs in one chain run together.** `.Then()` starts the next step, where Framer Motion would use keyframes or a sequence.
- **Animations stop when the element leaves the panel,** the way Framer Motion stops on unmount.
- **There is no layout animation (FLIP).** The `Width`, `Height`, `Top` and `Left` verbs animate layout values directly.

---

# Best animation library for Unity UI Toolkit: Cascade vs PrimeTween vs LitMotion
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/compare-primetween-litmotion.html

If you search for a way to animate Unity UI Toolkit, three libraries come up: PrimeTween, LitMotion and Cascade. All three can fade and move a `VisualElement`. They were built for different jobs, and that shows once your UI gets bigger than one button.

**Disclosure:** I make Cascade. I've tried to be fair to the other two. Every claim about PrimeTween and LitMotion below comes from their source code and docs (PrimeTween 1.5.2, LitMotion 2.0.2, checked November 2026). The Cascade version is 1.2. Every code sample on this page was compiled and run in one Unity 6000.4 project with all three libraries installed, and checked against what the text says it does. If something is wrong or out of date, tell me and I'll fix the page.

## The short answer

- **Your project already uses PrimeTween or LitMotion for gameplay:** use the same library for simple UI Toolkit tweens. One tween library is easier than two.
- **You need the fastest possible tweens for thousands of objects:** LitMotion (Burst and the Job System) or PrimeTween. In my UI Toolkit benchmark below, LitMotion was the fastest, Cascade second and PrimeTween third.
- **Your UI is built in UI Toolkit and has a lot of motion** (screens that come and go, lists, interruptible buttons, springs): Cascade was written for exactly that.
- **You write most of your UI code with an AI assistant:** Cascade is the only one of the three with official assistant support. See [AI coding assistants](#ai-coding-assistants).
- **You're on Unity 2022 or older:** Cascade needs Unity 6, so pick PrimeTween or LitMotion.

## At a glance

|  | PrimeTween | LitMotion | Cascade |
|---|---|---|---|
| Built for | Transforms, materials, uGUI, also UI Toolkit | Any value, very fast (DOTS) | UI Toolkit only |
| Price | free (PRO edition $32.99 adds Inspector animations) | free | Lite free; Pro paid |
| License | custom (free for commercial use) | MIT | Lite MIT; Pro Asset Store EULA |
| Unity | 2018.4+ (per its package) | 2021.3+ | 6000.0+ |
| Dependencies | none | Burst, Collections, Mathematics | none |
| UI Toolkit tweens built in | opacity, color, background color, translate/rotate/scale, left/top/width/height | opacity, colors, translate, scale, rotate, transform-origin, left/right/top/bottom, width/height, font size, text, progress bar | opacity, translate, scale, rotate, colors, width/height, left/top/right/bottom, border radius/width/color, font size, padding, background-image tint, slide-in from an edge, any float |
| Other styles | `Tween.Custom` | `Bind` | `Value` |
| Sequencing | yes (`Sequence`) | yes (`LSequence`, since 2.0) | yes (`Then()`, `At(seconds)`) |
| Await | yes | yes | yes |
| Physics springs | no (elastic/overshoot easing) | no (elastic easing) | Pro |
| Stagger helper | no (use delays) | no (use delays) | Pro |
| Shake / punch | Transform only | yes (float/Vector values, bind to any style) | yes: `Shake`, `Punch` (Lite); `PunchScale`, `PunchRotate`, `Pulse`, `Wiggle`, `Pop` (Pro). Additive, always end at rest |
| Stops when the element leaves the panel | no (measured: keeps writing to it) | no (measured: keeps writing to it) | yes |
| Reduced motion setting | no | no | yes (Lite and Pro) |
| AI coding assistant support | no official support (community-made agent skills exist) | no official support (community-made agent skills exist) | official agent skill, AI guide in the package, compile-time code checks; Pro: validated JSON animations |
| Screen transitions, hover/press, no-code component | no | no (the Inspector component has no UI Toolkit tracks) | Pro |

## The same animation in all three

A panel fades in while it slides up 40 px, a common way to show a window.

### PrimeTween

```csharp
using PrimeTween;

Tween.VisualElementOpacity(panel, startValue: 0f, endValue: 1f, duration: 0.3f, ease: Ease.OutCubic);
Tween.Position(panel, startValue: new Vector3(0, 40, 0), endValue: Vector3.zero, duration: 0.3f, ease: Ease.OutCubic);
```

`Tween.Position`, `Rotation` and `Scale` accept a `VisualElement` and write `style.translate`, `rotate` and `scale` on Unity 6.2 and newer.

### LitMotion

```csharp
using LitMotion;
using LitMotion.Extensions;

LMotion.Create(0f, 1f, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic).BindToStyleOpacity(panel);
LMotion.Create(new Vector2(0, 40), Vector2.zero, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic).BindToStyleTranslate(panel);
```

Every motion takes an explicit start value. LitMotion has the widest set of built-in style bindings of the three.

### Cascade

```csharp
using Cascade;

panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
     .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(40f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
```

Without `From()`, Cascade starts from the value the element has on the frame the animation begins, including values that come from USS.

## A sequence: fade in, then pop

### PrimeTween

```csharp
Sequence.Create()
    .Chain(Tween.VisualElementOpacity(panel, startValue: 0f, endValue: 1f, duration: 0.2f))
    .Chain(Tween.Scale(panel, endValue: new Vector3(1.1f, 1.1f, 1f), duration: 0.2f, ease: Ease.OutBack))
    .ChainCallback(() => Debug.Log("done"));
```

### LitMotion

```csharp
LSequence.Create()
    .Append(LMotion.Create(0f, 1f, 0.2f).BindToStyleOpacity(panel))
    .Append(LMotion.Create(Vector3.one, new Vector3(1.1f, 1.1f, 1f), 0.2f).WithEase(Ease.OutBack).BindToStyleScale(panel))
    .Run(b => b.WithOnComplete(() => Debug.Log("done")));
```

### Cascade

```csharp
panel.Animate()
     .Fade(1f, 0.2f).From(0f)
     .Then()
     .ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.2f).Ease(Ease.OutBack)
     .OnComplete(() => Debug.Log("done"));
```

All three read well. All three can also place a tween at an exact time inside a sequence: PrimeTween and LitMotion with `Insert`, Cascade with `At(seconds)`.

## Where the differences show up

### When the element leaves the screen

PrimeTween stops a tween when its target is a destroyed `UnityEngine.Object`, and LitMotion links motions to a GameObject with `AddTo`. A `VisualElement` isn't a Unity object, so neither check applies. Neither library listens for an element being removed from its panel, so when a screen closes or a list row is recycled mid-tween, stop it yourself. I measured it: a 2-second fade, with the element removed after 0.3 s, keeps changing the removed element's opacity in both libraries.

```csharp
// PrimeTween
panel.RegisterCallback<DetachFromPanelEvent>(_ => Tween.StopAll(onTarget: panel));

// LitMotion: keep the handles and cancel them
panel.RegisterCallback<DetachFromPanelEvent>(_ => handle.TryCancel());
```

Cascade cancels an animation when its element leaves the panel and never writes to an element that isn't displayed. In a UI with many screens, that's the bug class I most wanted to remove.

### Interrupting an animation

Buttons and drawers get interrupted all the time: hover out before the hover-in finishes, close a drawer while it's opening. With PrimeTween or LitMotion you stop the old tween and start a new one, usually from the current value. The new tween starts from rest, so the motion visibly loses its momentum.

Cascade Pro has physics springs. A spring that gets a new target keeps its current velocity, so the motion bends toward the new target instead of restarting:

```csharp
drawer.Animate().MoveX(open ? 0f : -320f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy);
```

Neither PrimeTween nor LitMotion has a velocity-based spring. Their elastic and overshoot easings look springy on a single run, but they restart on interruption.

### Lists

Making ten items enter one after another is a loop with a growing delay in PrimeTween (`startDelay`) or LitMotion (`WithDelay`). That works well. Cascade Pro has a helper for it:

```csharp
items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(16f).Stagger(0.05f);
```

### Reduced motion

Cascade has a global setting, `MotionSettings.Mode`: `Reduced` shortens animations and removes bounce, `Crossfade` replaces movement with fades, and `None` jumps to the end state but still fires `OnComplete`, so code that waits on an animation keeps working. Connect it to a "reduce motion" option in your settings menu. PrimeTween and LitMotion have no equivalent; you'd add the checks yourself.

### AI coding assistants

A lot of UI code is now written by asking Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or Codex. How well that goes depends on what the assistant knows about the library.

**PrimeTween and LitMotion** have been public since 2023 and 2024, so assistants have seen plenty of code that uses them. Neither project ships official assistant material, but community-made agent skills for both exist on GitHub. The catch for UI Toolkit is that most of that code animates Transforms, so assistants tend to reach for `transform` APIs, and don't know which VisualElement methods exist in the version you have.

**Cascade** is new, so an assistant without help will guess its API. To fix that, it ships three things:

- **An official agent skill** (`npx skills add twitchedd/cascade-skill`) for any agent that reads SKILL.md files. It checks whether your project has Lite or Pro and writes only code that tier can compile.
- **An AI guide inside the package** (`Documentation~/AI-GUIDE.md`, both tiers), so the assistant reads instructions that match your installed version.
- **Validated JSON animations** (Pro). An assistant can describe an effect as JSON; `SequencePreset.Validate` returns the exact step, field and a suggested fix for a typo, and `Lint` flags animations that would do nothing, such as a fade-in without a start value. The assistant can correct itself before you ever press Play.

Here's what that looks like. An assistant writes this entrance, with a verb name that doesn't exist:

```json
{ "steps": [ { "actions": [
  { "verb": "SlideIn", "edge": "Bottom", "distance": 40, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" },
  { "verb": "FadeIn", "to": 1, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" }
] } ] }
```

`Validate` says where the mistake is and what to use instead:

```csharp
MotionError err = SequencePreset.Validate(json);
// err.Path       → steps[0].actions[1].verb
// err.Suggestion → Fade
```

After the assistant renames it to `Fade`, the JSON is valid, but the fade still has no start value, so it would fade to where it already is and nothing would appear to happen. `LintSummary` catches that:

```text
steps[0].actions[1]: 'Fade' animates to 1, which is where the element already rests, and nothing earlier in this sequence moved it — so this action will run and change nothing — add "from" to say where it starts (e.g. "from": 0), or drop the action
```

Adding `"from": 0` clears both checks. All three messages above are the real output of Cascade.

I tested how much this matters. Claude Opus 5.5, running headless in Claude Code with no web access, wrote six common UI Toolkit animations: a panel entrance, a fade-then-pop sequence, a staggered list, a drawer that can be reversed mid-move, an endless pulse that stops when the element is removed, and an error shake. Every answer was compiled and run in Unity against a check for each task. When an answer failed, the compiler errors or failed checks went back to the model until it passed, and every token of every round was counted. Each setup ran 10 times.

The first round caught three mistakes in Cascade's own AI guide. It didn't say that `Loop()` repeats only the step right before it, it called `Delay()` a wait when it delays the step before it, and one example used a method overload that doesn't exist. Only 5 of 10 Cascade answers were right first time. I fixed the guide in the current Cascade 1.2, and the numbers below are from the fixed guide.

Each library got the setup you'd give it in practice. PrimeTween and LitMotion ship no assistant setup, so the model got each library's official docs plus a list of its UI Toolkit methods, and separately no docs at all, since it already knows both. Cascade ran in a Unity project with the package installed and its **Set Up AI Assistants** menu already run, which writes a short Cascade section into `CLAUDE.md` pointing at the guide in the package. Its prompt didn't mention any docs.

| Setup | Right first time | Output tokens | Cost per run | Lines of code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cascade 1.2, set-up project** | 10/10 | **1,546** | $0.14 | **42** |
| PrimeTween + its docs | 10/10 | 4,841 | $0.38 | 87 |
| LitMotion + its docs | 10/10 | 3,636 | $0.25 | 115 |
| PrimeTween, no docs | 10/10 | 3,466 | $0.14 | 90 |
| LitMotion, no docs | 10/10 | 2,866 | **$0.12** | 104 |
| No library (plain UI Toolkit) | 10/10 | 3,932 | $0.15 | 163 |

The numbers are medians of 10 runs. Cost is what Claude Code reported, at list API prices.

A bigger task tells the same story: a settings screen with a modal that can be reopened while it's closing, a toggle, a toast that stays up while it's re-triggered, a number that counts up, and press feedback. Each setup ran 5 times:

| Setup | Right first time | Output tokens | Cost per run | Lines of code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cascade 1.2, set-up project** | 5/5 | **6,659** | **$0.29** | **153** |
| PrimeTween + its docs | 5/5 | 11,046 | $0.56 | 212 |
| LitMotion + its docs | 5/5 | 10,134 | $0.43 | 251 |
| No library (plain UI Toolkit) | 5/5 | 9,422 | $0.31 | 310 |

What I take from it:

- Every setup got every task right in the end, so this compares cost, not ability.
- Cascade's answers were the shortest and used the fewest output tokens, because one fluent call covers what takes a loop or a helper in the others.
- In dollars, a set-up Cascade project cost about the same as plain UI Toolkit or PrimeTween without docs. LitMotion without docs was the cheapest on the small tasks, about 13% cheaper than Cascade. Giving PrimeTween or LitMotion their docs made them the most expensive, because reading the docs is most of the cost.

Here's one Cascade answer, exactly as the model wrote it:

```csharp
public static void EnterPanel(VisualElement panel)
{
    panel.Animate()
        .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic)
        .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(40f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}

public static void FadeThenPop(VisualElement panel, Action onDone)
{
    panel.Animate()
        .Fade(1f, 0.2f).From(0f)
        .Then()
        .ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.2f).From(1f).Ease(Ease.OutBack)
        .OnComplete(onDone);
}

public static void StaggerIn(IList<VisualElement> items)
{
    // From(0) is applied to every item immediately, so not-yet-started items stay invisible.
    items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Stagger(0.05f);
}

public static void SetDrawerOpen(VisualElement drawer, bool open)
{
    // MoveX replaces any running MoveX and continues from the current value.
    drawer.Animate().MoveX(open ? 0f : -320f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
}

public static void PulseForever(VisualElement badge)
{
    // Cascade cancels animations automatically when the element leaves the panel.
    badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.5f).From(1f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong);
}

public static void ShakeOnError(VisualElement field)
{
    field.Animate().Shake(10f, 0.4f);
}
```

This was the prompt for PrimeTween with docs. The others changed only the library name and namespace. The no-docs runs replaced the docs sentence with “You have no documentation for the library: write it from what you already know about its API.” Cascade's runs had no docs sentence, and the plain UI Toolkit runs were told to use only built-in UI Toolkit APIs.

```text
Using PrimeTween 1.5.2 (com.kyrylokuzyk.primetween), complete the six tasks in tasks.md (read it). Use the namespace AiTok.s_PTdocs_01. The file docs.md in this folder is the library's documentation; read it first and rely on it. Do not search the web. Write your answer as a single C# file named Tasks.cs in the current folder, then reply with one line saying you are done.
```

And the six tasks it was given (tasks.md):

```text
# Six Unity UI Toolkit animation tasks

Write one C# file that compiles in a Unity 6 project with the library installed. Use this exact shape
(replace NAMESPACE with the namespace you were given; keep the class and method names and signatures):

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UIElements;
// add the library's using directives

namespace NAMESPACE
{
    public static class Tasks
    {
        public static void EnterPanel(VisualElement panel) { ... }
        public static void FadeThenPop(VisualElement panel, Action onDone) { ... }
        public static void StaggerIn(IList<VisualElement> items) { ... }
        public static void SetDrawerOpen(VisualElement drawer, bool open) { ... }
        public static void PulseForever(VisualElement badge) { ... }
        public static void ShakeOnError(VisualElement field) { ... }
    }
}
```

All elements are already in a visible UIDocument panel. Durations are in seconds. Each method starts the
animation and returns immediately (no blocking, no coroutines that the caller must start).

1. **EnterPanel**: the panel fades in from opacity 0 to 1 and slides up from 40 px below its resting
   position (translate Y from 40 to 0), both over 0.3 s with an ease-out cubic curve.
2. **FadeThenPop**: fade the panel from opacity 0 to 1 over 0.2 s; when that finishes, scale it from 1 to
   1.1 over 0.2 s with an "out back" ease; when the scale finishes, call `onDone` exactly once.
3. **StaggerIn**: every item fades from opacity 0 to 1 over 0.3 s. Item i starts 0.05 × i seconds after
   item 0 (item 0 starts immediately). Items that haven't started yet must be invisible (opacity 0).
4. **SetDrawerOpen**: move the drawer horizontally (translate X) to 0 when `open` is true and to -320 when
   false, over 0.3 s with an ease-out curve. It may be called again while the previous call is still
   animating: the drawer must then continue smoothly from wherever it is now (no jump) to the new target,
   and the old animation must not keep fighting it.
5. **PulseForever**: scale the badge from 1 to 1.1 and back, continuously (0.5 s each way), forever. When
   the badge is removed from the hierarchy, the animation must stop (nothing keeps writing to it).
6. **ShakeOnError**: shake the field horizontally (translate X), up to about 10 px either side, for about
   0.4 s, ending exactly at translate X = 0 (it starts at 0).
```

It's one model in one tool, Claude Code with Opus 5.5, so other assistants may land differently. Where medians are within a few cents of each other (Cascade, PrimeTween without docs, plain UI Toolkit), the run-to-run ranges overlap, so treat those as about equal.

Details are on the [AI assistants page](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/ai-and-skill.html).

### Raw speed

LitMotion runs on Burst, and PrimeTween is built to make zero allocations. I measured all three on UI Toolkit: a release (Mono) player on an Apple M-series Mac, N elements each animating opacity and translate X back and forth forever, the same curve and timing in every library, 5 seconds measured after a 2-second warm-up, 3 runs each. The numbers are the extra milliseconds per frame over the same elements with no animation:

| Elements | PrimeTween | LitMotion | Cascade |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.1 ms | 0.1 ms | 0.1 ms |
| 500 | 0.5 ms | 0.3 ms | 0.4 ms |
| 1,000 | 0.8 ms | 0.5 ms | 0.7 ms |
| 2,000 | 1.5 ms | 0.9 ms | 1.3 ms |

None of the three allocated any memory per frame. The player's frame timer moves in 0.1 ms steps, so treat a difference of 0.1 ms as a tie. LitMotion is the fastest, Cascade is in between, and for typical UI, where tens of elements move at once, the difference doesn't matter: all three cost about 0.1 ms.

## Where Cascade is the weaker choice

- **Unity 6 only.** Projects on 2022 LTS or older can't use it.
- **UI Toolkit only.** It doesn't animate Transforms, uGUI or materials. If you need those too, you'll have a second library anyway.
- **Springs, stagger, transitions and the no-code component are paid.** PrimeTween and LitMotion are free. Cascade Lite is free and MIT licensed, and covers the tweens, sequences, await and reduced motion.
- **Younger and smaller.** PrimeTween and LitMotion have years of use and large communities. Cascade launched in 2026.
- **Assistants don't know it by default.** With no setup, an assistant guesses Cascade's API, while it already knows PrimeTween and LitMotion. One menu in the package fixes that, but it's a step the other two don't need.

## Which one should you pick?

- **A few UI Toolkit tweens in a game that already uses PrimeTween or LitMotion:** keep it.
- **Performance-critical tweening of many objects:** LitMotion.
- **A simple, free, well-documented tween API for everything:** PrimeTween.
- **A UI Toolkit interface with a lot of motion:** start with [Cascade Lite (free)](https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/slug/394764), and move to [Cascade Pro](https://assetstore.unity.com/packages/slug/394760) if you need springs, stagger or screen transitions.

## Sources

- PrimeTween: [GitHub](https://github.com/KyryloKuzyk/PrimeTween) (README, changelog, benchmarks) and the 1.5.2 package source.
- LitMotion: [GitHub](https://github.com/annulusgames/LitMotion) (2.0.2 source, `LitMotionUIToolkitExtensions.cs`) and [its docs](https://annulusgames.github.io/LitMotion/).
- Cascade: [these docs](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/index.html) and the [API reference](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/api.html).

---

# UI Toolkit animation performance: zero GC, lifecycle safety and channels in Cascade
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/performance.html

What Cascade does every frame, what it costs, and what happens to an animation when the UI around it changes.

## What runs each frame

- One scheduler tick per UI panel drives every animation on that panel. Cascade doesn't use `Update()`, coroutines or a MonoBehaviour.
- **No per-frame garbage.** Tweens are pooled and reused, and the update loop makes no allocations. The test suite checks this by measuring GC allocations while stepping many animations.
- Values are computed in plain C# and written to `style`. Cascade doesn't depend on Unity's experimental animation API.
- Animations run on unscaled time, so a paused game (`Time.timeScale = 0`) still animates its pause menu.

## Cheap and expensive properties

| Verbs | Property | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `Fade`, `MoveX/Y/To`, `Nudge`, `ScaleTo`, `Rotate`, `SlideIn` | opacity and transforms | cheap: no layout |
| `BackgroundColor`, `TextColor` | colors | cheap: repaint only |
| `Width`, `Height`, `Size`, `Top`, `Left` | layout | re-runs layout each frame |
| `BlurTo`, `TintTo` (Pro, Unity 6.3+) | filter | an extra render pass each frame |

Animate many elements with the cheap verbs. Use the layout verbs where the box really has to resize, such as an accordion.

For very large groups, such as hundreds of grid cells, Pro's `AnimateAll` and `StaggerFade` run one shared animation for the whole group instead of one per element. See the [API reference](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/api.html#VisualElementAnimationExtensions).

## When the element leaves the screen

An animation cancels itself when its element is removed from the panel, for example when a screen closes or a list row is recycled. Cascade never writes to an element that is no longer displayed. A cancelled animation doesn't call `OnComplete`; `OnSettled` receives `false`, and `await` returns `false`.

## Starting a new animation on a moving element

Each property is a **channel**: opacity, translate X, translate Y, scale, rotate, width, height, top, left. Starting a new animation on a channel replaces the one already running on it, from the current value, so there is no jump. Other channels keep going: a new fade doesn't stop a move.

A replaced animation counts as cancelled, so it never calls `OnComplete`. Use `OnSettled` for anything that must happen either way. In Pro, a replaced spring hands its velocity to the new animation.

`Nudge`, `NudgeX` and `NudgeY` don't claim a channel. They add on top of whatever is moving the element.

## Stopping

```csharp
var h = el.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.3f);
h.Cancel();                                       // this animation
el.StopAnimations();                              // everything on the element
el.StopAnimations(MotionChannel.Opacity);         // one property; the rest keeps going
```

Stopping leaves the element where it is. An animation that reaches its end on its own snaps exactly to its target.

## Measuring

```csharp
Debug.Log(MotionSettings.Stats);   // active panels, sequences and tweens, plus pooled tweens
```

`MotionSettings.Stats` is allocation-free. Show it on a debug overlay, or check in a test that animations really stopped.

## Platforms

Cascade is pure C# with no native code and no dependencies. It runs wherever UI Toolkit runs in Unity 6000.0 and later. Each release is tested in the editor and in a built standalone player.

---

# Animate Unity UI Toolkit with AI: the Cascade agent skill and JSON sequences
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/ai-and-skill.html

Cascade is built to be written by AI coding assistants as well as people. The API is small and regular, the package ships a guide written for assistants, and Pro can play animations described as validated JSON.

## Install the Cascade agent skill

The skill teaches a coding agent how to use Cascade: which calls exist, the mistakes to avoid, and how to check its own output. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot and any agent that reads `SKILL.md` files.

```sh
npx skills add twitchedd/cascade-skill
```

Or copy `skills/cascade/` from the repository into your agent's skills folder (for Claude Code: `.claude/skills/cascade/`).

Skill on GitHub Skill on skills.sh

### It writes code for your tier

The skill first checks `Packages/manifest.json` to see whether the project has Cascade Lite or Cascade Pro, and writes only code that tier can compile. Ask a Lite project for a bouncy spring and it says springs are in Pro and offers the closest Lite version, an `Ease.OutBack` overshoot.

### Things to ask it

- "Make the settings panel slide up and fade in when it opens."
- "Stagger the inventory slots in from the right."
- "Make this button pop when pressed."
- "Shake the gold counter when the player can't afford an item."
- "Respect reduced motion in all our menu animations."

## The AI guide inside the package

Both tiers ship `Documentation~/AI-GUIDE.md`, written for assistants: every verb, the easing names, what happens when a new animation interrupts a running one, the rules that prevent the common mistakes, and examples from intent to code. Pro keeps the JSON format in `AI-GUIDE-JSON.md` beside it, so an assistant writing C# reads only what it needs. Because the guide comes with the package, it always matches the version you have installed. The skill reads it when it exists. Without the skill, point your assistant at it:

```text
Read Packages/com.twitched.cascade.lite/Documentation~/AI-GUIDE.md,
then fade the shop panel in when it opens.
```

(For Pro the folder is `Packages/com.twitched.cascade/`.)

### One-click setup Pro

**Tools > Cascade > Set Up AI Assistants** writes a short Cascade section into the files coding assistants read from your project folder: `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md` and `.cursor/rules/cascade.mdc`. It points them at the guide for your installed version, so you don't have to. Files you already have keep their content; only a marked Cascade section is added or replaced. Run it again after upgrading Cascade.

### The rule assistants most often miss

Every verb animates to a value, starting from the element's current value. "Fade in" on an element that is already visible animates from 1 to 1, and nothing happens. Entrances must state where they start:

```csharp
panel.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);   // not just Fade(1f, 0.3f)
```

The guide and the skill both teach this, and Pro's linter (below) catches it.

The second most common: `.Delay()` and `.Loop()` change only the step right before them. `.Loop()` after a `.Then()` chain repeats the last step, not the chain, so a pulse is one step that ping-pongs:

```csharp
badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.1f, 0.5f).From(1f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong);
```

## JSON animation sequences Pro

For self-contained effects such as an entrance, a shake or a pulse, an assistant can describe the animation as JSON instead of code. JSON is constrained and checked before it runs, so a mistake produces a precise error instead of code that fails to compile.

```json
{ "steps": [ { "actions": [
  { "verb": "SlideIn", "edge": "Bottom", "distance": 40, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" },
  { "verb": "Fade", "from": 0, "to": 1, "duration": 0.4, "ease": "OutCubic" }
] } ] }
```

Steps run one after another; the actions inside a step run together. Durations are in seconds.

```csharp
using Cascade;

SequencePreset.PlayJson(panel, json);                                   // parse and play

if (SequencePreset.TryFromJson(json, out var preset, out string error))  // or check first
    preset.Play(panel);
else
    Debug.LogWarning(error);   // e.g. "step 0, action 1: verb 'Fade' requires a numeric "to""
```

### Let the assistant fix its own output

Errors name the exact step, action and field, and suggest the closest valid name for a typo, so an assistant can correct the JSON and try again:

```csharp
MotionError err = SequencePreset.Validate(json);
if (err.IsError)
{
    // err.Code: UnknownVerb, MissingField, OutOfRange, ...
    // err.Path: "steps[0].actions[1].to"
    // err.Suggestion: "Fade" for a misspelled verb, otherwise null
}

foreach (var advice in SequencePreset.Lint(json))   // valid, but would do nothing
    Debug.Log(advice);                             // e.g. a fade-in without "from"
```

`Validate` answers "will this run". `Lint` answers "will this do what was meant", for example a fade-in on an element that is already visible.

The full format is in a JSON Schema you can give to a model or a validator: [cascade-sequence.schema.json](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/cascade-sequence.schema.json).

### From JSON to the inspector

A generated sequence can be saved as a preset asset, and designers pick it in the **UI Animator** component's rules without writing code. The `Documentation~` folder includes `PROMPTS.md`, a set of ready-made intents with their JSON.

## For AI search and crawlers

This site publishes [llms.txt](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/../../llms.txt), a plain-text index of these docs for language models and AI search tools.

---

# Easing curves for Unity UI Toolkit animation: every Cascade ease, drawn
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/easing.html

An ease shapes the speed of an animation over its duration. Every curve below is in both Lite and Pro, under `Ease`.

```csharp
panel.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0.4f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);
```

## Which one to use

- **Entrances:** `OutCubic` (the default) or `OutQuart`. Fast start, soft landing.
- **Exits:** `InCubic`. Accelerating away reads as "gone".
- **Moving between two places on screen:** `InOutCubic`.
- **Pop-ins and dialogs:** `OutBack` for a small overshoot (or a [spring](https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/spring-animation.html) in Pro).
- **Loops and pulses:** `InOutSine` with `LoopMode.PingPong`.
- **Progress and spinners:** `Linear`.

## All curves

The two lines mark the start and end values. Curves that cross them overshoot.

`Ease.Linear`Constant speed. Mechanical; use for progress bars and spinners. `Ease.InSine` `Ease.OutSine` `Ease.InOutSine`Gentle both ends. Good for looping pulses. `Ease.InQuad` `Ease.OutQuad` `Ease.InOutQuad` `Ease.InCubic`Accelerates away. Good for exits. `Ease.OutCubic`Fast start, soft landing. The default for entrances. `Ease.InOutCubic`For moves between two resting places. `Ease.InQuart` `Ease.OutQuart` `Ease.InOutQuart` `Ease.InExpo` `Ease.OutExpo`Very fast start, long settle. `Ease.InOutExpo` `Ease.InCirc` `Ease.OutCirc` `Ease.InOutCirc` `Ease.InBack`Pulls back before leaving. `Ease.OutBack`Overshoots slightly, then settles. Dialogs and pop-ins. `Ease.InOutBack` `Ease.InElastic` `Ease.OutElastic`Wobbles into place. Playful rewards. `Ease.InOutElastic` `Ease.InBounce` `Ease.OutBounce`Lands and bounces. A drop or a falling badge. `Ease.InOutBounce` Your own curve Draw a curve in the inspector and use it as an ease:

```csharp
[SerializeField] AnimationCurve curve = AnimationCurve.EaseInOut(0, 0, 1, 1);

badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.2f, 0.5f).Ease(Ease.FromCurve(curve));
```

The curve is sampled from time 0 to 1. Values above 1 or below 0 overshoot.

## Easing in the inspector and JSON

Presets and JSON sequences name the ease as text (`"ease": "OutBack"`). They accept this subset: Linear, InSine, OutSine, InOutSine, InQuad, OutQuad, InOutQuad, InCubic, OutCubic, InOutCubic, OutQuart, OutExpo, OutCirc, InBack, OutBack, InOutBack, OutElastic, OutBounce. Code can use all of the curves above.

---

# Cascade API reference: Unity UI Toolkit animation (C#)
Source: https://twitchedd.github.io/cascade/docs/api.html

Every public type and member, generated from the comments in the source. Members marked Lite are in both tiers; everything else is Pro.

All types are in the `Cascade` namespace. Durations are in seconds.

- [Start an animation](#start-an-animation)
- [The animation handle](#the-animation-handle)
- [Easing](#easing)
- [Springs](#springs)
- [Stagger](#stagger)
- [Transitions](#transitions)
- [Hover, press and focus](#hover-press-and-focus)
- [Named states](#named-states)
- [Settings and accessibility](#settings-and-accessibility)
- [JSON sequences and presets](#json-sequences-and-presets)
- [Effects](#effects)

## Start an animation

### `VisualElementAnimationExtensions` class Lite

Entry points for the fluent API. These are the only symbols most users touch.`element.Animate()…` returns a `TweenSequence` you can chain and keep as a handle.

```csharp
static TweenSequence Animate(this VisualElement element)
```

(Lite) Begin a fluent animation on this element. The returned `TweenSequence` is both the builder and the control handle. Dispatch is deferred to the next scheduler tick.

```csharp
static void StopAnimations(this VisualElement element)
```

(Lite) Cancel every Cascade animation currently running on this element.

```csharp
static bool StopAnimations(this VisualElement element, MotionChannel channel)
```

(Lite) Stop animating ONE property of this element, e.g. `el.StopAnimations(MotionChannel.Opacity)` freezes a running fade at its current value while a simultaneous move keeps going. O(1) via the engine's channel-claim registry. Only the cancelled tween is affected: it goes inert but keeps its place in the sequence timeline, so siblings keep running, `.Then()` steps still start at their authored time, and the sequence's `OnComplete` still fires (at the authored time) when something in it finishes naturally, unless the cancelled channel was the sequence's only content (then it's a cancel: no OnComplete, per the engine's Cancel ≠ complete rule). Scope caveats: this stops the tween **currently animating** that channel, a tween still in its `.Delay()`, queued in a later `.Then()` step, or dispatched this frame has no channel claim yet, is not targetable (returns false), and will play at its authored time as a separate animation. Closure-mode verbs (SlideIn/MoveTo/colors) have no channel identity, use `StopAnimations` for those.Returns: True when a live animation on that channel was stopped.

```csharp
static StaggerBuilder AnimateEach(this IEnumerable<VisualElement> elements)
```

Begin a staggered animation across a collection of elements: The same chain plays on every element, with element `i` offset by `i * stagger`.

```csharp
static TweenSequence AnimateAll( this IEnumerable<VisualElement> elements, Func<VisualElement, float> captureFrom, float to, Action<VisualElement, float> apply, float duration, float stagger, EaseFunction ease = null, MotionChannel channel = MotionChannel.Custom)
```

**Coalesced** staggered animation: one tween samples a shared eased curve and fans the value across every element (each offset by `i * stagger`), instead of one independent tween per element. At 500-element scale that's ONE runner slot + one `resolvedStyle` read per element (captured once at start) rather than N tweens each re-stepping, far less dirty-flag and bookkeeping churn. Returns the group handle (pause/cancel the whole stagger at once). `captureFrom` reads each element's start value (captured at that element's own start, not the group's); `apply` writes the interpolated value; both run per element. The element collection is snapshotted at call time. For the common case use `StaggerFade`. **The group lasts `duration + (count-1) * stagger`, not `duration`.** A fixed per-element stagger therefore scales with the collection, see `Stagger` for `TotalDuration` (to schedule after a group) and `StepForSpan` (to pin its length). The group is ONE tween on the shared host, so cancelling it needs this handle; `StopAnimations()` on a member element will not stop it.Returns: The group handle, or `null` when `elements` is null/empty (no-op).

```csharp
static TweenSequence AnimateAll( this IEnumerable<VisualElement> elements, Func<VisualElement, Color> captureFrom, Color to, Action<VisualElement, Color> apply, float duration, float stagger, EaseFunction ease = null, MotionChannel channel = MotionChannel.Custom)
```

Coalesced staggered **colour** sweep, the same machinery as the float `AnimateAll`, but capturing and interpolating a `Color` per element. This overload exists because the obvious way to write a colour sweep with the float version is wrong in a way that looks right. Lerping from `resolvedStyle.backgroundColor` inside the apply callback reads the value the previous frame wrote, so each frame blends a shorter remaining distance and the colour converges early instead of travelling the curve, it merely looks like a soft ease, which is why it ships. Here the start colour is captured once, at each element's own start, exactly like every other verb.Returns: The group handle, keep it if anything else will later write these elements, because a coalesced group is ONE tween hosted on the shared parent and `StopAnimations()` on an individual element does not reach it.

```csharp
static TweenSequence StaggerFade(this IEnumerable<VisualElement> elements, float to, float duration, float stagger, EaseFunction ease = null)
```

Coalesced staggered opacity fade across `elements`, the cascade list entrance. One tween for the whole group (see `AnimateAll`).

## The animation handle

### `TweenSequence` class Lite

What `Animate()` returns: you chain verbs on it to build the animation, and keep it to control the animation (`Pause`, `Resume`, `Cancel`, `await`). Verbs add to the current step and run together; `Then()` starts the next step. The animation starts on the element's next frame, so everything you chain in the same line applies.

```csharp
TweenSequence Fade(float to, float duration)
```

(Lite) Animate `opacity` to `to` over `duration` seconds.

```csharp
TweenSequence FadeTo(float to, float duration)
```

(Lite) Alias of `Fade`, matches the `FadeTo` name used by the Interaction and Variant APIs (and the JSON "Fade" verb's C# alias), so converting between them is mechanical.

```csharp
TweenSequence MoveX(float to, float duration)
```

(Lite) Animate the X component of `style.translate` (pixels).

```csharp
TweenSequence MoveY(float to, float duration)
```

(Lite) Animate the Y component of `style.translate` (pixels).

```csharp
TweenSequence SlideIn(Edge edge, float duration, float distance = 48f)
```

(Lite) Slide the element in from a screen `edge`: it starts offset by `distance` px in that direction and animates `style.translate` to 0. Unlike the other verbs this uses an explicit "from" (the offset), and pre-positions the element immediately so there is no first-frame flash at its layout position. Pair with `Fade` for the classic cascading-menu entrance.

```csharp
TweenSequence ScaleTo(float to, float duration)
```

(Lite) Animate uniform `style.scale` to `to`.

```csharp
TweenSequence Scale(float to, float duration)
```

(Lite) Alias of `ScaleTo`, matches the JSON `"Scale"` verb name, so an AI converting JSON to fluent C# can use the same name instead of knowing the `ScaleTo` rename.

```csharp
TweenSequence Rotate(float toDegrees, float duration)
```

(Lite) Animate Z rotation (degrees) via `style.rotate`.

```csharp
TweenSequence MoveTo(Vector2 to, float duration)
```

(Lite) Animate `style.translate` to a target offset (pixels) on both axes at once.

```csharp
TweenSequence Nudge(float x, float y, float duration)
```

(Lite) Displace the element by `x`, `y` pixels and bring it straight back, the "your input was rejected" bump, a damage shake, an error wobble. **Additive, and that is the whole point.** A nudge does not claim TranslateX/Y, so it composes with whatever is already positioning the element instead of superseding it.
